Homework 3 : Exploratory Data Analysis & Visualization¶

Dataset: Seattle Police Department Crime Data (2008 – Present)

Student: Jeevitha Bandi

Course: DATA 5310 – Data Visualization

What is in this data set?¶

Check out this fantastic dataset! It contains crime reports from the Seattle Police Department, spanning from 2008 all the way to the present. Sourced from the City of Seattle Open Data portal, it offers a treasure trove of detailed information about crime incidents that can help us better understand what's happening in our neighborhoods.

Here are some of the key features you’ll find in the dataset:

  • Report Date: This tells us when each crime was recorded, helping us see trends over time.
  • Offense Parent Group: These are broad categories like Theft, Assault, and Burglary that help us group similar types of crimes.
  • Offense Type: This goes into the specifics of each crime, giving us a clearer picture of what happened.
  • MCPP Neighborhood: Each crime is categorized by community policing area, so we can dive into local crime patterns.
  • District / Sector: This indicates which patrol division responded, providing insights into law enforcement coverage in different areas.
  • Arrest Flag: This shows whether an arrest was made, which can help us understand how effectively law enforcement is addressing crime.
  • Latitude / Longitude: These coordinates offer the approximate location of each incident, making it easier to visualize crime hotspots.
  • Year, Month, Hour: These details allow us to analyze how crime varies over time and even by the hour.

This dataset is perfect for digging into crime trends, exploring differences across neighborhoods, and understanding patterns around arrests. By using this valuable information, we can collaborate to make Seattle a safer place for everyone!

Cleaning data¶

In [5]:
# Converting Report DateTime to datetime
df["Report DateTime"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Report DateTime"], errors="coerce")

# Creating new time-based columns
df["Year"] = df["Report DateTime"].dt.year
df["Month"] = df["Report DateTime"].dt.month
df["Hour"] = df["Report DateTime"].dt.hour

Reported Crimes per Year in Seattle (2008–2025)

This bar chart presents the total number of reported crimes in Seattle from 2008 to 2025. We can see that crime rates fluctuated between 75,000 and 90,000 incidents per year, with a peak in 2018 and 2019. Notably, there was a significant decline in 2020 and 2021, likely due to changes in public activity during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The chart uses bar heights effectively for quick comparisons and maintains a clean design, focusing only on the relevant years. This makes it easy to understand the trends in Seattle's crime rates over time.

Top 10 Crime Types in Seattle (2008–2025)

Check out this bar chart showing the ten most common crime types reported in Seattle from 2008 to 2025! It's interesting to see that Theft from Motor Vehicles and Burglary/Breaking & Entering appear as the most frequent offenses. Vandalism, Simple Assault, and Shoplifting follow closely behind. Overall, property-related crimes outnumber violent ones, suggesting that many of Seattle's public safety challenges might be more about economic factors or opportunistic situations.

The design of the chart focuses on simplicity and clarity, using bar length to effectively represent the data. With a single color scheme and a minimalist style, it really emphasizes the information, making it easy to read and understand.

#Plot 3 – Crimes by Hour of Day
plt.figure(figsize=(10,5))
sns.countplot(x="Hour", data=df, color="coral")
plt.title("Crimes by Hour of Day (2008–2025)")
plt.xlabel("Hour of the Day (0–23)")
plt.ylabel("Number of Reports")
plt.show()

This bar chart provides an interesting look at how reported crimes change throughout the day. You’ll notice that there’s a significant rise in incidents during the late morning and early afternoon, peaking around 1 PM. After that, things start to calm down as we head into the evening and nighttime. It's also worth mentioning that very few crimes are reported between 2 AM and 6 AM, which probably reflects how quiet it gets during those hours.

The way the hours are laid out on the x-axis makes it easy to see the trends over time. Plus, the consistent color scheme and simple design really follow good practices for clear data presentation. The height of the bars does a great job of showing how many incidents there are, which aligns well with how we naturally perceive differences in size.

In [23]:
# Aggregate counts by hour into a tidy DataFrame
hourly = df.groupby("Hour").size().reset_index(name="Count").sort_values("Hour")

# Line plot from the tidy frame
plt.figure(figsize=(10,5))
sns.lineplot(data=hourly, x="Hour", y="Count", marker="o", color="crimson")
plt.title("Hourly Trend of Crimes in Seattle (2008–2025)")
plt.xlabel("Hour of the Day (0–23)")
plt.ylabel("Number of Reports")
plt.xticks(range(0,24))
plt.show()

This line chart displays the hourly distribution of reported crimes in Seattle. The pattern shows that criminal activity remains low between 2 AM and 6 AM, then rises sharply through the morning hours, peaking around 1 PM. After mid-afternoon, the number of incidents gradually decreases into the evening.

By connecting data points with a line, this visualization better highlights the continuous nature of time compared to the earlier bar chart. The use of position on a common scale and slope (Cleveland & McGill, 1985) makes trends easy to perceive, while the minimalist layout follows Tufte’s data-ink principles, ensuring clarity and focus on the data rather than design embellishment.

Preliminary graphics¶

Question 1: How have property crimes changed over time in Seattle (2008–2025)?

In [51]:
# Filtering only Property crimes
property_crimes = df[df["NIBRS Crime Against Category"] == "PROPERTY"]

plt.figure(figsize=(10,5))
sns.countplot(x="Year", data=property_crimes, color="steelblue")
plt.title("Trend of Property Crimes in Seattle (2008–2025)")
plt.xlabel("Year")
plt.ylabel("Number of Property Crime Reports")
plt.xticks(rotation=45)
plt.show()

Property crimes in Seattle gradually increased through the early 2010s, peaking around 2018–2020, and then declined sharply during the 2020–2022 period. This drop coincides with the COVID-19 pandemic, which likely reduced public activity and opportunities for theft and burglary. The overall trend suggests that property crimes are sensitive to social and economic disruptions, as normal activity resumed after 2021, the numbers began to stabilize but did not fully return to pre-pandemic highs.

From a design standpoint, this bar chart is highly effective because the bars clearly convey year-to-year differences in magnitude. The encoding (position along a common scale) provides accurate visual comparison, and the consistent color keeps focus on temporal change rather than style. The trend is compelling because it shows a meaningful, real-world pattern that aligns with historical events.

Q2 and Q3 are below Refined Graphics section

Refined Graphics for Q1¶

In [43]:
#Iteration 1 - Baseline (Bar Chart)
plt.figure(figsize=(10,5))
sns.countplot(x="Year", data=property_crimes, color="steelblue")
plt.title("Trend of Property Crimes in Seattle (2008–2025)")
plt.xlabel("Year")
plt.ylabel("Number of Property Crime Reports")
plt.xticks(rotation=45)
plt.show()

This bar chart provides a clear year-to-year view of property crime counts. It’s readable and straightforward but somewhat “blocky,” making it hard to perceive smooth changes over time. The design is accurate but could benefit from better temporal encoding, using a continuous mark like a line to emphasize trend direction.

In [44]:
#Iteration 2 – Changing Bar Chart to Line Plot
# Aggregate yearly totals
property_yearly = property_crimes.groupby("Year").size().reset_index(name="Count")

plt.figure(figsize=(10,5))
sns.lineplot(data=property_yearly, x="Year", y="Count", marker="o", color="steelblue")
plt.title("Yearly Trend of Property Crimes in Seattle (2008–2025)")
plt.xlabel("Year")
plt.ylabel("Number of Reports")
plt.show()

Line Plot: Showing Continuity Over Time

Switching from a bar chart to a line plot effectively underscores the continuous nature of yearly changes, rather than treating each year as an isolated category. By connecting the data points, we can see the trend more clearly: property crimes rose consistently from 2012 to 2018, peaked around 2020, and then began to decline. This design enhances expressiveness, as the line format better illustrates the flow over time, while the straightforward colors and point markers keep the focus squarely on the data itself. Overall, the graphic is clear, accurate, and easy to interpret, aligning with Mackinlay’s (1986) principle of matching data types with appropriate visual representations.

In [45]:
#Iteration 3 – Add Color Encoding for Change
plt.figure(figsize=(10,5))

# Creating a Boolean column for increase/decrease
property_yearly["Trend"] = property_yearly["Count"].diff() > 0

# Plot gray base line
sns.lineplot(data=property_yearly, x="Year", y="Count", color="gray", marker="o")

# Overlay colored points for increases/decreases
sns.scatterplot(
    data=property_yearly,
    x="Year",
    y="Count",
    hue="Trend",
    palette={True: "green", False: "red"},
    s=100,
    legend=False
)

plt.title("Property Crimes in Seattle (2008–2025): Increases (Green) and Decreases (Red)")
plt.xlabel("Year")
plt.ylabel("Number of Reports")
plt.show()

In this version, red and green markers highlight the years with increases or decreases in reported crimes. This color coding offers an immediate visual cue for the direction of change, allowing viewers to grasp the information quickly without needing to closely examine the numeric labels. By adding a second variable, direction to the plot, while maintaining the original position encoding, the presentation becomes more effective. However, the introduction of color can slightly increase cognitive load and rely on individual color perception. Therefore, while color can enhance emphasis, it should always be paired with clear labeling when used in formal communications.

In [48]:
#Iteration 4 - Smoothed Trend of Property Crimes in Seattle (2008–2025)
plt.figure(figsize=(10,5))
sns.regplot(data=property_yearly, x="Year", y="Count",
            scatter=True, color="navy", line_kws={"color": "orange"})
plt.title("Smoothed Trend of Property Crimes in Seattle (2008–2025)")
plt.xlabel("Year")
plt.ylabel("Number of Property Crime Reports")
plt.show()

I used sns.regplot() to create a regression plot that illustrates a linear trend line for yearly property crime data.

The orange line reflects the estimated average trend in property crime reports from 2008 to 2025. The navy blue dots represent the actual counts of incidents each year, while the light orange shaded area indicates the confidence interval, which helps us understand the uncertainty surrounding that estimated trend.

Starting around 47,000 reports in 2008, property crimes fluctuated over the years but showed a slight upward trend according to the regression line. However, the actual data reveals peaks around 2020, followed by a significant drop in 2025. This suggests that while the linear model captures the overall direction, it may smooth out short-term fluctuations.

Additionally, the widening shaded region towards the right indicates greater uncertainty in the later years, largely because the data for 2025 may be incomplete or volatile.

In [50]:
#Iteration 5 - Final Refined Graphic with Annotation
plt.figure(figsize=(10,5))

# Line plot
sns.lineplot(data=property_yearly, x="Year", y="Count",
             marker="o", color="steelblue", linewidth=2)

# Adjusting title and layout to prevent overlap
plt.title("Property Crimes in Seattle (2008–2025): Sharp Decline During Pandemic", pad=20)
plt.xlabel("Year")
plt.ylabel("Number of Reports")

# Adding annotation with spacing
pandemic_year = property_yearly[property_yearly["Year"] == 2020]
plt.text(
    pandemic_year["Year"].values[0] + 0.2,  # move slightly to the right
    pandemic_year["Count"].values[0] + 1500,  # move text above the point
    "Pandemic-related decline begins ->",
    color="darkred",
    fontsize=10,
    ha="left"
)

# Adjusting figure spacing
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The plot features a clean line design, avoiding regression smoothing to highlight the actual data trends clearly.

Utilizing a steel blue line with circular markers ensures visual consistency throughout the chart.

The annotation (“Pandemic-related decline begins ->”) provides valuable context and emphasizes a key social event that impacted the data: the COVID-19 pandemic of 2020.

By positioning the text (ha="right", with an offset of +1500), it prevents overlap with the data point, thus maintaining readability.

Property crimes show a gradual increase from 2012 to 2018, peaking around 2020.

Following this peak, there’s a noticeable drop, which coincides with the pandemic year, likely a result of reduced mobility, fewer operational businesses, and lockdown measures.

From a design standpoint, this chart effectively narrates a story, rather than merely presenting data; the annotation links a visible trend to its probable cause.

The simple blue hue keeps consistency with previous versions while drawing attention to the annotation.

Question 2: At what time of day are crimes most frequently reported in Seattle?

In [28]:
plt.figure(figsize=(10,5))
sns.countplot(x="Hour", data=df, color="coral")
plt.title("Crimes by Hour of the Day (2008–2025)")
plt.xlabel("Hour of Day (0–23)")
plt.ylabel("Number of Reports")
plt.show()

This bar chart illustrates the number of crime reports logged throughout the 24 hours of a day. Overnight, the reports remain low but start to pick up after 7 AM, reaching their peak around midday before steadily declining in the evening. The graphic effectively addresses the question at hand, as the sequential order on the x-axis allows for easy interpretation of hourly patterns. However, while the general trend of activity is evident, it lacks a certain depth since the chart does not differentiate between types of crime. Additional grouping, for instance, by property versus violent crimes, could provide a more insightful view of the trends.

Overall, the visualization is striking and informative, it highlights the city's crime hotspots and prompts further exploration of the social or environmental factors that may contribute to these issues.

Summary of Refined Graphic: Property Crimes in Seattle (2008 – 2025)¶

Over the course of five versions, our visualization transformed from a simple bar chart into a clear, annotated line plot that really highlights the trend and context of property crimes in Seattle.

We started with basic bars to establish a baseline, but quickly realized that a continuous line would better capture how things changed over time. Adding color helped us show year-to-year ups and downs, and we even included a regression line to illustrate the overall trend amidst the yearly fluctuations.

In the final version, we added an annotation to point out the decline in crimes related to the pandemic, which shifted our chart from just being descriptive to actually telling a story. Each adjustment we made was guided by key visual principles, like using position along a common scale, color for emphasis, and minimizing unnecessary details, to boost clarity and understanding.

The end result is a concise and engaging narrative: property crimes steadily increased through the 2010s, peaked around 2020, and then took a sharp dive during the pandemic years. This shows just how powerful thoughtful visual design can be in enhancing our understanding and telling compelling stories!

Conclusion¶

This assignment was a fantastic journey into how exploratory visualization can uncover meaningful insights from real-world data, specifically looking at Seattle crime reports from 2008 to 2025.

From the start, diving into basic graphics helped me see how different visual elements, like bar length, position, and color, can effectively showcase changes over time, location, and categories. By exploring three key questions, I was able to better understand how property crimes, daily timing, and neighborhood dynamics shape the city's safety.

One of the most exciting parts was refining my graphics. I transformed a simple bar chart into a detailed line plot, which really highlighted the importance of thoughtful design. With each new version, I added clarity, context, and visual precision, inspired by the principles of Tufte and Cleveland & McGill, who emphasize how important it is to minimize visual clutter and enhance perceptual accuracy.

Ultimately, this experience taught me that visualization goes beyond just displaying numbers, it's about creating a clear, evidence-based story. By the end, I not only gained a deeper understanding of Seattle’s crime trends but also developed a greater appreciation for how intentional design choices can turn raw data into engaging narratives.
